## Overview

"Hard Examples Are All You Need" investigates whether example difficulty affects GRPO training effectiveness by comparing selection strategies (easy, medium, hard, random) across multiple models and reasoning tasks.

## Key Findings

Training on the hardest 10% of examples yields dramatic performance gains up to 47%, while easy examples produce minimal improvements of 3-15%. This occurs because GRPO requires outcome variance to generate learning signals; hard examples maintain mixed success/failure outcomes throughout training while easy examples quickly converge to consistent success, eliminating learning opportunities.

## Generalization Results

Training on the hardest examples not only improves in-distribution performance, but is also the only strategy that yields meaningful gains on OOD data. Specifically, models trained on hard examples show superior out-of-distribution generalization, with only hard-trained models achieving meaningful gains on the AIME2025 benchmark.

## Experimental Setup

The experiments were conducted on GSM8K grade-school math problems and BIG-Bench Hard's Tracking Shuffled Objects task across models including Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-14B, Phi-4, and Llama3.1-8B.

The paper is available on arXiv (2508.14094) and was posted in August-October 2025.

## Overview

PEAR (Policy Evaluation-inspired Algorithm for Offline Learning Loss Re-weighting) is an SFT-stage method that corrects distribution mismatch and better prepares models for RL.

## The Problem

Models initialized from stronger SFT checkpoints can significantly underperform those initialized from weaker ones after identical RL training, due to a mismatch between the distribution that generates offline SFT data and the policy optimized during online RL, which learns from its own rollouts.

## The Solution

PEAR uses importance sampling to reweight the SFT loss, with three variants operating at the token, block, and sequence levels. It can be used to augment standard SFT objectives and incurs little additional training overhead once probabilities for the offline data are collected.

## Results

PEAR consistently improves post-RL performance over canonical SFT, with pass at 8 gains up to a 14.6 percent on AIME2025. The paper conducts controlled experiments on verifiable reasoning games and mathematical reasoning tasks on Qwen 2.5 and 3 and DeepSeek-distilled models.

The paper was published on February 1, 2026.

**Paper Title:** "Quagmires in SFT-RL Post-Training: When High SFT Scores Mislead and What to Use Instead"

**Main Contribution:**
The paper challenges whether high SFT (Supervised Fine-Tuning) scores translate to improved performance after RL, providing extensive counter-examples where this is not true.

**Key Findings:**
High SFT scores can be biased toward simpler or more homogeneous data and are not reliably predictive of subsequent RL gains or scaled-up post-training effectiveness. In some cases, RL training on models with improved SFT performance could lead to substantially worse outcome compared to RL on the base model without SFT.

**The Problem:**
The lack of predictability for final performance after RL from pre-RL models leads to quagmires for post-training, where SFT teams may provide suboptimal RL learners and creates frictions between post-training teams owning different SFT and RL stages.

**Solution Proposed:**
The researchers identify generalization loss on held-out reasoning examples and Pass@large k performance to provide strong proxies for the RL outcome.

The paper was submitted on October 2, 2025 and is available on arXiv at 2510.01624.

## Overview

The paper addresses how reinforcement learning (RL) has proven effective in incentivizing the reasoning abilities of large language models (LLMs), but suffers from severe efficiency challenges due to its trial-and-error nature.

## The Problem with Two-Stage Training

The common practice of employing supervised fine-tuning (SFT) as a warm-up stage for RL suffers from catastrophic forgetting: second-stage RL gradually loses SFT-acquired behaviors and inefficiently explores new patterns.

## The Proposed Solution

The paper introduces BRIDGE, a novel method for training large language models to enhance their reasoning capabilities by enabling a cooperative interaction between Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning (RL).

The study introduces a method employing bilevel optimization to facilitate better cooperation between training paradigms. By conditioning the SFT objective on the optimal RL policy, the approach enables SFT to meta-learn how to guide RL's optimization process. During training, the lower level performs RL updates while simultaneously receiving SFT supervision, and the upper level explicitly maximizes the cooperative gain—the performance advantage of joint SFT-RL training over RL alone.

The paper was submitted to arXiv on September 8, 2025, with a revised version on October 16, 2025.

## DC-SFT: Difficulty-Curated SFT

Difficulty-Curated SFT (DC-SFT) is a method that explicitly filters the training set based on sample difficulty.

### Key Findings

The research proposes that RL's generalization advantage arises from an implicit data filtering mechanism that inherently prioritizes medium-difficulty training samples. Training on hard samples significantly degrades out-of-distribution (OOD) performance.

### Implementation

DC-SFT has two variants: SFT-M, which trains exclusively on medium-difficulty instances, and SFT-EM, which trains on both easy and medium-difficulty instances while removing only hard samples.

### Performance Results

DC-SFT substantially enhances OOD generalization over standard SFT and surpasses the performance of RL-based training, while providing greater stability and computational efficiency.

## Overview

Light-R1 is an open-source suite for training long reasoning models using reproducible and cost-effective methodology. Given the proprietary nature of data used in the DeepSeek-R1 series, the researchers develop an alternative approach leveraging exclusively public data and models.

## Training Approach

The curriculum training progressively increases data difficulty, combined with multi-staged post-training. The approach involves a curriculum-based training regimen incorporating Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Dual Policy Optimization (DPO), and reinforcement learning via GRPO.

## Key Results

The Light-R1-32B model, trained from Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, outperforms DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B in math reasoning. Additionally, fine-tuning DeepSeek-R1-Distilled models with 3,000 challenging examples from the curriculum dataset yielded state-of-the-art 7B and 14B models, while the 32B model, Light-R1-32B-DS performed comparably to QwQ-32B and DeepSeek-R1.

The paper was submitted on March 13, 2025, with the latest version (v4) on May 28, 2025.
